title: Ukrainian diaspora
summary: The Ukrainian diaspora consists of Ukrainians and their descendants living outside [[ukraine|Ukraine]], who often maintain connections to their ancestral homeland and a sense of Ukrainian national identity. This diaspora is widespread, particularly in post-Soviet states, North America, and parts of Europe and South America.

sections.heading: Distribution
paragraphs: The Ukrainian diaspora is present in various countries globally, with significant concentrations in [[post-soviet-states|post-Soviet states]] such as Belarus, Kazakhstan, Moldova, and Russia, as well as in Central Europe (the Czech Republic, Germany, and Poland), North America (Canada and the United States), and South America (Argentina and Brazil).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The Ukrainian diaspora has a complex history, beginning with political emigration after the Battle of [[poltava|Poltava]] in 1709, when some [[cossacks|Cossacks]] settled in Turkey and Western Europe. Subsequent waves of emigration occurred after the fall of the [[zaporizhian-sich|Zaporozhian Sich]] in 1775, leading to [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] settlements in regions such as Dobruja and the Volga.

By 1880, the Ukrainian diaspora numbered approximately 1.2 million, with a significant presence in the Russian Empire and Austro-Hungary. The late 19th century saw a surge in emigration to the Americas, particularly influenced by Dr. Joseph Oleskiw's advocacy for Ukrainian agricultural settlers to move to Canada.

Before World War I, nearly 500,000 [[ukrainians|Ukrainians]] had emigrated to the Americas, with the diaspora in the US, Canada, and South America growing significantly. By 1914, the Ukrainian diaspora in the Americas was estimated to be between 700,000 and 750,000.

The diaspora played a crucial role in advocating for Ukrainian independence during the tumultuous years surrounding World War I and the Russian Civil War, leading to the establishment of various Ukrainian organizations and cultural institutions abroad.

sections.heading: Post-World War Developments
paragraphs: Following World War I and the Russian Civil War, a significant political emigration occurred, bolstering Ukrainian communities in Western and Central Europe. This period saw the establishment of Ukrainian universities and organizations that aimed to support the independence movement.

The 1920s and 1930s witnessed further emigration driven by economic factors, with many Ukrainians leaving for the Americas and Western Europe. By the early 1930s, the diaspora outside [[soviet-union|the Soviet Union]] was estimated at 1.7-1.8 million.
After World War II, a second wave of Ukrainian emigration occurred, with approximately 250,000 displaced persons settling in Germany and Austria, further expanding the Ukrainian diaspora.
